prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty.

statement.case_for: After reading all eight openings I move B025 from fourth place on my own ballot to my preferred single-achievement prize. The criterion I quoted in March is a discovery or invention with a named originator, and the lattice clock fits it: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the trade-off between atom number and motional or light-shift systematics, and the first strontium lattice clocks followed from it. Ye's group then took the concept to roughly 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, with the stability and many-body control that made the comparisons meaningful. Maturity is as strong as anything on the list: independent clocks in several countries agree at that level, the redefinition of the second is under discussion, and the clocks are already used for tests of constants and relativistic geodesy. It is also the only candidate that all eight members ranked, with four in their top three, so it is the one case in which opening support reflects a broadly shared judgment rather than one subfield's enthusiasm. I treat that as a signal to test, not as merit, and the merit argument above stands without it. The two-name credit list is compact and matches what every proposer who named laureates wrote.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is category and overlap. Some will call this a metrology and instrument advance rather than a discovery of a new phenomenon, and the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems sit close by, so the committee must state clearly what is new. Attribution at the margin is also real: Lemonde, Ludlow, Gill, Sterr, Takamoto and others contributed to the early strontium demonstrations and to the stability record and are outside the credited names. If the committee wants a prize that opens a new field of matter rather than a measurement capability, B022 or B036 are the natural alternatives, and I do not claim B025 is the uniquely correct choice. My own first-place B008 has only my support and a direct connection to my field, so I do not press it as the preferred configuration.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B025 fifth, calling it very high impact but a metrology story rather than a new phenomenon, and suggested that Jun Ye's possible overlap with the thorium nuclear clock favours crediting him only once.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-instrument point seriously, since I make it about my own B008. But the criterion is discovery or invention, and the magic-wavelength lattice clock is a specific, attributable invention whose consequences were qualitatively new: tests of constants and geodesy at 1e-18 that no earlier standard allowed. I also read the thorium-229 isomer work as premature, since a working nuclear clock has not yet matched lattice performance, so I do not see Ye's credit being split. His credit here rests on the lattice clock accuracy and stability work, not on a candidate I would not support. I do agree that the 2005 and 2012 prizes require a careful citation, which is why I tie mine to the lattice concept.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B022 fourth and judged the interpretation not yet stable and the timing somewhat early, given that the superconducting mechanism and phase diagram remain debated.
responses.response: I ranked B022 second and still regard it as a strong candidate, so this is a qualification rather than a rejection. The occurrence of correlated insulators and superconductivity is secure, but the pairing mechanism and sample dependence of twist-angle disorder mean the physics is less settled than for lattice clocks, whose agreement across independent laboratories is quantitative. That difference in maturity is why I put B025 ahead for this year. I would not dismiss B022 as premature, however: the theory-plus-experiment triple is clean and replication is broad, and I keep it as my first alternative. I part from Eriksson only in how much weight the unsettled mechanism should carry against a discovery that is otherwise secure.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first as the architecture beneath most superconducting processors and as a natural sequel to the 2025 circuits prize, while admitting a four-name credit problem and his own proximity to the community.
responses.response: I ranked B016 sixth and my reservations are the ones he lists. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits is recent and close, so a second circuit award in the very next cycle needs a distinct scope statement that I do not yet see. Also, Schoelkopf, Wallraff, Blais and Girvin are four names for three places, and several members cut a different name, so the attribution is unresolved. I agree that maturity and originality are high and that his candour about proximity is appropriate. My difference is about timing and the cut, not about the quality of the idea. I would want the committee to settle who is excluded before B016 can displace a better-attributed candidate.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B025 first, arguing that magic-wavelength lattices removed Doppler and recoil shifts for many atoms at once, that independent laboratories confirm 1e-18, and that the two-name credit is compact and fair.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this and it moved my ranking. His point about many atoms interrogated at once without motional shifts is the clearest statement of why the invention changed what could be measured. I would add one qualification to his attribution: his own note that Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and others contributed to the stability record means the citation should name the concept and its realisation at the highest accuracy, not claim the whole field. I also note he relied on recalled uncertainty figures, as did I, and I treat the 1e-18 value as something the committee should verify against the primary comparisons before the citation is fixed.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a discovery or invention distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes.
How to weigh the early strontium contributions of Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Ludlow and others against the two credited names.
Whether the 2025 circuits prize makes B016 too close this year, and whether B022 is mature enough to outrank a clock prize.
The 1e-18 figures and the chronology of the first lattice clocks are from recollection and unverified here.
statement.conflict_note: I have a documented institutional connection to Japan through a JSPS fellowship, a University of Tokyo fellowship and long-running exchanges with Japanese universities. Hidetoshi Katori is, to my recollection, at the University of Tokyo, so this may warrant a recusal check, although nothing in my profile documents a collaboration or co-authorship with him or with Jun Ye. Separately, my own first-place B008 lies in my own field of electron microscopy, and I have discounted my enthusiasm for it. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson favours B016, which I did not rank first, so I see no conflict there.
